Female Greater bulldog bats attain a maximum adult body mass of approximately 56 grams [Wwi = approximately 56 grams], whereas males are noticeably heavier, reaching an ultimate wet weight of about 67 grams [Wwi = about 67 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is among the most extreme recorded in the family Noctilionidae and likely reflects the selective pressures associated with male-male competition for roosting and foraging territories. Newborn pups emerge at a remarkably precocial state, with a wet weight at birth of roughly 7.8 grams [Wwb = roughly 7.8 grams], a value that represents about 14 percent of the average female's adult mass and is substantially larger than the altricial neonates of many insectivorous bat lineages. The substantial birth mass is thought to facilitate rapid early development and a relatively brief period of dependency on maternal care.

The reproductive output of this species is constrained to a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], and females produce exactly one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year], making for a very modest annual fecundity rate typical of slow-lived tropical mammals. This low reproductive tempo is paired with an extended gestation period measured in captive colonies maintained at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], where pregnancy has been documented to last approximately 180 days [tg = approximately 180 days]. Such a lengthy gestation is exceptional among bats of comparable body mass and is more reminiscent of the prolonged intrauterine development observed in some phyllostomid frugivores. The substantial investment in each individual offspring, combined with the long interval between successive litters, underscores a life-history strategy prioritizing offspring quality and survival over high reproductive turnover.

Weaning represents a critical nutritional transition for the growing young, which become independent of maternal milk after roughly 31 days [tx = roughly 31 days] at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This relatively short lactation period, considering the large birth mass, suggests that the pups progress rapidly from suckling to the consumption of whole fish captured by the mother. Following weaning, the juveniles enter a protracted sub-adult phase before achieving full reproductive capacity. Data derived from comparative studies of the congener Natalus mexicanus indicate that time since birth at puberty in Noctilio leporinus is approximately 365 days [tp = approximately 365 days] when raised under controlled thermal conditions at 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C]. This delayed sexual maturation aligns with the species' extended lifespan and slow life-history pace.

Basal metabolic measurements obtained from resting individuals under thermoneutral conditions at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C] reveal a maximum oxygen consumption of 47.00 milliliters per hour [JOi = 47.00 milliliters per hour], a value consistent with the elevated energetic demands of a piscivorous diet and active hunting over open water. This metabolic rate, though modest in absolute terms due to the species' moderate body size, is relatively high when scaled allometrically compared to insectivorous bats of similar mass, reflecting the costly neuromuscular coordination and sensory processing required for aerial prey capture from water surfaces. The maintenance of such a high resting metabolism is supported by the energy-rich fish diet and the bats' habit of foraging in large, productive aquatic habitats.

Longevity records for wild populations indicate that Noctilio leporinus can survive for approximately 11.8 years [am = approximately 11.8 years] at 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a lifespan consistent with the slow life-history syndrome characterized by low annual fecundity and late sexual maturation. This maximum documented lifespan is notably longer than predicted by body mass alone, reinforcing the pattern that piscivorous bats, like their frugivorous counterparts, tend to be longer-lived than insectivorous species of equivalent size. The combination of a single annual pup, a six-month gestation, delayed puberty approaching one year after birth, and a decade-long reproductive window allows sufficient time for the species to maintain stable populations despite the high energetic costs of piscivory and the challenges of locating suitable foraging habitats.
